hints: Think about what makes any amine or ammonia basic at the particle level, focusing on the lone pair on nitrogen.
Compare the cyclohexyl group with just a hydrogen atom in ammonia, thinking about whether an alkyl group pushes electrons toward or away from nitrogen.
Compare phenylamine with ammonia by picturing where the nitrogen lone pair can go when it is directly attached to a benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Picture what basic means for nitrogen**
Think of a base as a lone pair looking for a proton. All three compounds, $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$, have one lone pair on nitrogen. The more electron rich and available that lone pair is, the stronger the base and the more readily $\text{RNH}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{RNH}_3^+$ occurs.

See why cyclohexylamine beats ammonia**
The cyclohexyl ring is an alkyl group. Alkyl groups push electrons toward nitrogen by the positive inductive effect. That puts extra electron density onto N in cyclohexylamine compared with $\text{NH}_3$, so its lone pair is more ready to bond to $\text{H}^+$. That is why an aliphatic amine is more basic than ammonia.

See why phenylamine is weakest**
In phenylamine the nitrogen is attached directly to a benzene ring. The lone pair in the nitrogen p orbital can overlap with the ring pi system and become delocalised into the ring. Once spread into the ring, it is much less available to pick up a proton. So phenylamine is a much weaker base than ammonia, giving the order cyclohexylamine > ammonia > phenylamine.

Final answer: cyclohexylamine > ammonia > phenylamine, most basic to least basic.
Basicity depends on availability of the nitrogen lone pair to accept a proton / donate to a proton.
The cyclohexyl / alkyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect, increasing electron density on N, so lone pair more available.
In phenylamine the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised / overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring, decreasing electron density on N, so lone pair less available.

hints: Recall the two stage name used when a nucleophile attacks a $\text{C=O}$ in an acyl chloride and then $\text{Cl}^-$ leaves.
walkthrough:
Recognise the two stages at the carbonyl**
You have $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ reacting with an amine to give an amide. First the amine adds to the $\text{C=O}$ carbon to form a tetrahedral intermediate, then the $\text{Cl}$ leaves as $\text{Cl}^-$. That two stage pattern for acyl compounds is called nucleophilic addition-elimination.

hints: Start by identifying the nucleophile and the electrophile, thinking about the lone pair on $\text{R-NH}_2$ and the polarity of $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$.
Remember how to draw the first curly arrow from a lone pair to an electron deficient carbon, and the paired arrow from the double bond onto oxygen.
Think about what charges appear in the middle structure when N forms a new bond and O gains the $\text{C=O}$ electrons.
Consider how the intermediate collapses back to $\text{C=O}$ by pushing electrons onto the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to expel $\text{Cl}^-$.
walkthrough:
Set up the nucleophile and electrophile**
Draw $\text{R-}\overset{..}{\text{N}}\text{H}_2$ with its lone pair clearly shown. In $\text{CH}_3\text{C(=O)Cl}$ mark the carbonyl as $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ because oxygen pulls the electrons away. That $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ is the target for the nitrogen lone pair.

Draw the addition step**
Push a curly arrow from the nitrogen lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. At the same time push a curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ bond onto O. This forms a new $\text{N-C}$ bond and gives a tetrahedral intermediate: $\text{R-N}^+\text{H}_2-\text{C}(\text{O}^-)(\text{CH}_3)\text{Cl}$. Notice N becomes positive because it has used its lone pair to make four bonds, and O becomes negative with three lone pairs.

Draw the elimination step**
Now the $\text{O}^-$ lone pair swings back to reform $\text{C=O}$. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to the $\text{C-O}$ bond. To keep carbon with four bonds, the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond must break. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to Cl, expelling $\text{Cl}^-$. Later proton transfer steps give the neutral amide $\text{R-NH-CO-CH}_3$ plus $\text{HCl}$.

Final answer: First step: lone pair on N of $\text{R-NH}_2$ attacks $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$; curly arrow N lone pair to C, curly arrow $\text{C=O}$ to O.
Intermediate: $\text{R-N}^+\text{H}_2-\text{C}(\text{O}^-)(\text{CH}_3)\text{Cl}$ with $\text{N}^+$, $\text{O}^-$ and lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ shown.
Second step: lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ reforms $\text{C=O}$, curly arrow $\text{O}^-$ to $\text{C-O}$ bond, curly arrow $\text{C-Cl}$ to Cl to expel $\text{Cl}^-$.

hints: Compare the formula of amide L with the given formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{17}\text{NO}_2$ to work out what extra $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ fragment has been added and what has been lost from N.
walkthrough:
Spot the second acylation on nitrogen**
Amide L is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NHCOCH}_3$. It still has one $\text{N-H}$. With excess $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ that $\text{N-H}$ can react again in the same addition-elimination way. Replace the remaining H on N with a second $\text{COCH}_3$ group to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{N}(\text{COCH}_3)_2$. That adds $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ overall, matching $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{17}\text{NO}_2$, a diacyl amine (imide).
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{N}(\text{COCH}_3)_2$ : N-cyclohexyl-N-acetyl acetamide, with two $\text{CH}_3\text{C=O}$ groups both bonded to N which is bonded to the cyclohexyl ring.
